Aluminum (Anodized Red). Aluminum can be colorized by a process called anodization. It creates a layer of aluminum oxide by supplying different voltages which results in different thickness. Unlike titanium, aluminum doesn't get vivid colors from anodization so dyes are used to color it further. Source: Refractive index database.

Titanium (Anodized). Titanium can be colorized by a process called anodization. It creates a layer of titanium dioxide by supplying different voltages which results in different thickness and color. Additional colors can be achieved by adding dyes. Source: Refractive index database.

Honey (Crystallized). Variations in its water content alter its refractive index. Typically, the refractive index for honey ranges from 1.504 at 13% water content to 1.474 at 25%. Fresh honey is liquid and clear but with time it crystallizes and becomes thicker and less clear. The crystallization depends on temperature and the ratio of glucose and fructose. Source: Honey.
Ketchup. Source: A Practical Model for Subsurface Light Transport.
Lemon. Source: Spectral Materials Database.
Orange. Source: Spectrophotometer Measurement.

Glass (Borosilicate). Borosilicate glass has numerous advantages over regular soda-lime glass, including having a higher clarity (transparency). Borosilicate is generally slightly more expensive than soda-lime glass. Source: Refractive index database.

Glass (Soda-lime). Soda-lime glass is the most prevelant type of glass made, and accounts for about 90% of manufactured glass. It's used for windowpanes and glass containers (bottles and jars) for beverages, food, and some commodity items. Source: Refractive index database.

Blood (Deoxygenated). The color of blood depends on its oxygen level. When hemoglobin has a full oxygen load, it has a bright red color, and when it's deoxygenated it's a darker red. For example, arterial and capillary blood is bright, and venous blood is dark. Upon exposure to air, deoxygenated blood quickly oxygenates and turns a brighter shade of red. Source: Blood.

Blood (Oxygenated). The color of blood depends on its oxygen level. When hemoglobin has a full oxygen load, it has a bright red color, and when it's deoxygenated it's a darker red. For example, arterial and capillary blood is bright, and venous blood is dark. Upon exposure to air, deoxygenated blood quickly oxygenates and turns a brighter shade of red. Source: Blood.
Eye (Cornea). Source: Cornea.

Eye (Lens). The refractive index of human lens varies from approximately 1.406 in the central layers down to 1.386 in less dense layers of the lens. This index gradient enhances the optical power of the lens. Source: Lens (vertebrate anatomy).
Eye (Sclera). Source: Optical properties of human sclera in spectral range 370-2500 nm.

Beer (Pale Lager). While the index of refraction of beer depends on its alcohol and sugar contents, beer contains 90%-95% water, so the index of refraction can in most cases be assumed to be close to that of water. Source: Acquiring Scattering Properties Of Participating Media By Dilution.
Coffee. Source: Photo Reference.
Cola. Source: Acquiring Scattering Properties Of Participating Media By Dilution.
Cooking Oil. Source: Index of Refraction of Vegetable Oil.
Cream. Source: A Practical Model for Subsurface Light Transport.

Ethanol. Ethanol is also called ethyl alcohol, grain alcohol, drinking alcohol, or simply alcohol. The refractive index of an alcoholic beverage such as vodka depends on the ratio of alcohol and water. For example, vodka with 40% alcohol by volume contains 40% ethanol and 60% water. Source: Ethanol.
Gasoline. Source: Gasoline.

Honey (Liquid). Variations in its water content alter its refractive index. Typically, the refractive index for honey ranges from 1.504 at 13% water content to 1.474 at 25%. Fresh honey is liquid and clear but with time it crystallizes and becomes thicker and less clear. The crystallization depends on temperature and the ratio of glucose and fructose. Source: Honey.

Petroleum. The viscosity of crude oil is sensitive to temperature. Source: Petroleum.
Toothpaste. Source: Spectrophotometer Measurement.
Vodka (40%). The refractive index of vodka depends on the ratio of alcohol and water. Vodka with 40% alcohol by volume contains 40% ethanol and 60% water. Source: Vodka.

Water. While relatively small quantities of water appear to be colorless, pure water has a slight blue color that becomes deeper as the thickness of the observed sample increases beyond 50 cm. The hue of water is an intrinsic property and is caused by selective absorption and scattering of white light. Dissolved elements or suspended impurities may give water a different color. Source: Refractive index database.
Wine (Red). Source: Acquiring Scattering Properties Of Participating Media By Dilution.
Wine (White). Source: Acquiring Scattering Properties Of Participating Media By Dilution.
Asphalt (Fresh). Asphalt consists of crushed stone, gravel, and sand, bound together with bitumen. Source: Spectral Materials Database.

Concrete. Source: Feeding a Physically Based Shading Model.
Aluminum. Source: Refractive index database.

Brass. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, with a bright and gold-like appearance. It is similar to bronze, another alloy containing copper that uses tin instead of zinc. Historically, the distinction between the two alloys has been less consistent and clear, and modern practice in museums and archaeology increasingly avoids both terms for historical objects in favor of the more general "copper alloy". Source: Refractive index database.

Pearl. The akoya pearl is a saltwater cultured pearl from the akoya oyster. Akoya are considered to be the classic pearl used for necklaces and other pearl jewelry. Nacre is the material of which pearls are composed and consists of aragonite crystal layers separated by conchiolin, a protein secreted by mollusk shells. The thickness of these layers determines the color of reflection from the nacre. The transmission interference color is complementary to the reflection interference color. Source: Structural colors of pearls.

Soap Bubble. The colors of a soap bubble are the result of an interaction between the light reflected from the front and back surfaces of the soap film, a phenomenon known as thin-film interference. The thickness of a soap bubble can range between 10 nm and 1000 nm. It's thinner at the top due to gravity. Source: Soap Bubble Wiki - Color and Film Thickness.
Blackboard. Source: Spectral Materials Database.

Car Paint. Modern car paints are nearly always an acrylic polyurethane "enamel" with a pigmented basecoat and a clear topcoat. It may be described as "acrylic", "acrylic enamel", "urethane", etc. and the clearcoat in particular may be described as a lacquer. The size of the metal flakes in metallic paints is typically between 100 to 400 microns in diameter. Modern automobile paint is applied in several layers, with a total thickness of around 100 μm (0.1mm). Source: Automotive Paint.
Whiteboard. Source: Spectral Materials Database.
Cardboard. The material commonly referred to as "cardboard" is more specifically named "corrugated fiberboard". Source: Spectrophotometer Measurement.

Office Paper. Office paper contains optical brightening additives that absorb light in the ultraviolet and violet region (usually 340-370 nm), and re-emit light in the blue region (typically 420-470 nm) by fluorescence. Source: Spectrophotometer Measurement.
Toilet Paper. Source: Spectrophotometer Measurement.

Plastic (PC). Source: Polycarbonate.
Plastic (PET). Source: Polyethylene Terephthalate.
Plastic (PLA). Source: Polylactic Acid.

Plastic (PUR). Modern car paints are nearly always an acrylic polyurethane "enamel" with a pigmented basecoat and a clear topcoat. It may be described as "acrylic", "acrylic enamel", "urethane", etc. and the clearcoat in particular may be described as a lacquer. Source: Polyurethane.
Plastic (PVC). Source: Polyvinyl Chloride.

Gray Card. In photography and computer graphics, middle gray is a tone that is perceptually about halfway between black and white on a lightness scale. Light meters and cameras are often calibrated using an 18% gray card or a color reference card such as a ColorChecker. It is typically defined as 18% reflectance in visible light. Source: Gray Card.
MIT Black. Source: MIT engineers develop “blackest black” material to date.

Musou Black. Musou Black is one of the darkest paints available. Darker materials can be achieved by using carbon nanotube technology, such as the “MIT Black” material. Source: Spectrophotometer Measurement.
Rust. When iron reacts with oxygen it transforms into a non-metal substance called iron oxide. Source: Spectrophotometer Measurement.

Spectralon. Spectralon is a fluoropolymer that has the highest diffuse reflectance of any known material or coating over the ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared regions of the spectrum. It is the whitest substance available and reflects 99% of the light. Source: Spectralon.
Toner (Black). Black toner printed on office paper with linear sRGB values of 0, 0, 0. Source: Spectrophotometer Measurement.
Marble. Source: A Practical Model for Subsurface Light Transport.
